title: Feature Stores with Feast
intro: Training/serving skew happens when training computes a feature one way (in a notebook, from the warehouse) and serving computes it another way (in the API, from a live database). The model then sees different numbers in production than it learned on. A feature store defines each feature once and serves the same values to both. This tutorial covers the core Feast workflow in a repo that defines features for drivers.

steps.prompt: Preview what Feast would change in the registry and infrastructure from your feature definitions, without applying anything.
steps.fake_output:
Created entity driver
Created feature view driver_hourly_stats
Created sqlite table repo_driver_hourly_stats
steps.explanation: One entity (driver) and one feature view would be registered, plus an online-store table created.
steps.why: 'feast plan' is to 'feast apply' what 'terraform plan' is to 'terraform apply': review first, especially in CI, where a renamed feature view could drop an online table production reads from.

steps.fake_output:
Created entity driver
Created feature view driver_hourly_stats
Deploying infrastructure for driver_hourly_stats
steps.explanation: The definitions are now in the registry, the shared catalog every training job and service reads.
steps.why: The definition lives in version-controlled Python and the registry, not in someone's notebook. That shared definition is what removes skew: training and serving can't disagree about how conv_rate is computed if there's only one definition.

steps.prompt: List the registered feature views to confirm.
steps.explanation: driver_hourly_stats is registered against the driver entity.
steps.why: The registry is also discovery: before building a new feature, check whether another team already has it. Duplicated features that drift apart are another source of skew.

steps.prompt: Load the latest feature values from the offline store (the warehouse) into the online store (low-latency, for serving), up to now: materialize incrementally with the current UTC time.
steps.explanation: The online store now holds the latest values per driver, picking up from the last materialization.
steps.why: The offline store has full history (for training with point-in-time-correct joins); the online store holds only the latest value per entity (for millisecond lookups). Run materialize on a schedule. If it stops, serving quietly uses stale features while training data stays fresh: a new kind of skew, so alert on materialization lag.

steps.prompt: Start the Feast feature server locally so a model service can fetch features over HTTP.
steps.fake_output:
INFO: Started server process [4121]
INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:6566
steps.explanation: The feature server is up on port 6566.
steps.why: Serving features over HTTP (or through the Python SDK in-process) means the model service doesn't reimplement feature logic. It asks for 'conv_rate for driver 1001' and gets exactly what training used.

steps.prompt: Fetch online features for driver_id 1001: POST to localhost:6566/get-online-features with the JSON body in the file features.json.
steps.explanation: The same conv_rate and avg_daily_trips definitions that training used, served in milliseconds.
steps.why: Check the statuses: NOT_FOUND or OUTSIDE_MAX_AGE means the entity is missing or its value is older than the feature view's TTL. Serving code must handle that explicitly with a sensible default, rather than letting a null reach the model and silently produce garbage predictions.
